interviewQuestions.question: How do you check whether a single number is prime, and why do you only check up to its square root?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I check divisibility by every integer from 2 up to `sqrt(n)`, returning false the moment one divides evenly, and true if none do. The reason the square root is a safe stopping point: divisors of n always pair up as d and n/d. If both numbers in a pair exceeded `sqrt(n)`, their product would exceed n — so it's impossible for a divisor above the root to exist without a matching one below it. That means checking the lower half of the range is enough to catch every possible divisor.

A quick production version also special-cases 2 and 3, then only tests candidates of the form `6k - 1` and `6k + 1`, since every prime above 3 fits one of those forms — that cuts roughly two-thirds of the candidates without changing the complexity class, which stays **O(sqrt(n))**.

I'd also flag a subtle bug: comparing `i <= sqrt(n)` using a floating-point square root can misfire right at a perfect square boundary due to rounding, so I compare `i * i <= n` instead, which stays in exact integer arithmetic.

**Testing:** whether you can justify the square-root cutoff mathematically, not just recite it as a rule of thumb.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: When would you use the Sieve of Eratosthenes instead of just calling your primality-check function in a loop?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It comes down to how many queries I expect against a known upper bound N. Trial division per number costs O(sqrt(n)), so checking every number from 2 to N costs O(N * sqrt(N)) total. Building a sieve once costs O(N log log N) total and then answers any lookup in O(1). Once the number of queries against that bound starts to exceed roughly sqrt(N), the sieve's one-time build cost is already paid back.

The flip side matters just as much: if I only need to check one number, or the number is enormous (say 10^18) with no bounded range to precompute over, building a sieve is either wasted setup or physically impossible — a boolean array over 10^18 entries doesn't fit in any real machine's memory. In that case trial division or a probabilistic test like Miller-Rabin is the right call, even though it's asymptotically "worse" per check.

So my actual decision rule isn't "which algorithm is faster in isolation" — it's "what's the query pattern." A range-bounded, many-queries situation wants a sieve; a single large check wants trial division. I've seen candidates default to sieving reflexively because it's the more sophisticated-sounding answer, which is exactly backwards when there's only one query.

**Testing:** whether you choose an algorithm based on the actual access pattern rather than picking the most advanced-sounding tool by default.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: Your sieve implementation is correct but noticeably slower than a coworker's on the same N. What would you check first?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First thing I'd look at is where the inner marking loop starts. If it starts at `2 * p` instead of `p * p` for each prime p, the output is still correct — every composite still gets struck out eventually — but it's redoing work: any multiple of p below p*p already has a smaller prime factor and was already marked composite in an earlier pass. That's a correctness-preserving but measurably slower bug, and it's the single most common performance gap between two "working" sieve implementations. Across all primes up to N it moves the total cost from roughly O(N log log N) toward O(N log N).

Second, I'd check the outer loop bound — it should stop once `p * p > N`, not run all the way to N; continuing past `sqrt(N)` only re-scans numbers that are already resolved, since any composite up to N has a prime factor at or below `sqrt(N)`.

Third, I'd check memory layout: a boolean array of one byte per entry versus a packed bitset can be a meaningful constant-factor difference at large N, though it doesn't change the asymptotic class — same reasoning as Big-O never promising equal wall-clock time for equal complexity classes.

Because this bug produces a correct answer, it survives ordinary tests entirely and only shows up as a performance regression — which is exactly why I'd check the marking-loop start point before anything else.

**Testing:** whether you can debug a subtle performance-only bug that unit tests wouldn't catch, versus only knowing to check for outright wrong answers.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging

interviewQuestions.question: How would you find all primes between 2*10^9 and 2*10^9 + 10^6 without running out of memory?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd use a **segmented sieve** rather than a plain sieve starting from zero. A plain sieve over the full range up to 2*10^9 + 10^6 would need roughly 2 GB for a byte-per-entry boolean array — workable but wasteful, and it gets impossible fast if the upper bound were even a few orders of magnitude larger.

The segmented approach: first sieve small primes up to `sqrt(2*10^9 + 10^6)`, which is only around 44,722 — cheap, fast, and small enough to fit trivially in memory. Then allocate a boolean array sized only to the **window** (10^6 entries here, not the full range), and for each small prime, mark its multiples that fall inside the window rather than from 0.

The correctness argument is the same square-root fact from single-number primality: any composite number in the window must have a prime factor at or below `sqrt(upper bound)`, so the small-prime list from the first pass is guaranteed sufficient to strike out every composite in the window — nothing is missed by skipping the range below the window.

This is the standard technique for "primes in a range" competitive-programming and interview problems where the range doesn't start at zero and the absolute numbers are too large to sieve directly.

**Testing:** whether you know a technique beyond the textbook sieve for large or offset ranges, and can justify why it's still correct.
